java-reading-a-stack-trace.svg.title: Reading a Java error like a map
java-reading-a-stack-trace.svg.caption: Read the first line for the kind of problem, then walk down the list of calls until you reach a line from your own code. That is the place to open and fix.
steps: Red text appears. Do not panic, it is a clue.
It names the problem: NullPointerException, and often why.
Each one is a method that was running, newest at the top.
Lines from java.base or libraries are usually not the real cause.
Look for a line like Greeter.java:7. That is your code.
Look at the exact spot and ask: what could be null or wrong here?
Fix it, run again, and check that the error is gone.
A small test makes sure the bug never comes back.

java-array-boxes-and-index.svg.title: An array is a row of numbered boxes
java-array-boxes-and-index.svg.caption: The boxes are numbered from 0. The last box is length minus one. Asking for a number outside the row causes ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
steps: int[] scores = {5, 8, 3, 9, 1}; makes five boxes in a row.
scores[0] is the first box. Counting starts at zero.
scores[2] is the third box. You can read it or change it.
scores[4] is the last box, because length is 5 and 5 minus 1 is 4.
for (int i = 0; i < scores.length; i++) visits every box.
for (int s : scores) visits each value without an index.
Use an ArrayList. A plain array has a fixed size.

java-static-versus-instance.svg.title: Shared by the school, owned by the student
java-static-versus-instance.svg.caption: Static things belong to the class and are shared by every object. Instance things belong to one object. final means a value is set once and never changed.
steps: static int count counts every Student ever made.
new Student() creates one student with their own name.
Ben has a different name. Changing Ava does not change Ben.
count++ runs for each new student, so count becomes 2.
Student.count is 2, no matter which student you ask.
static final int MAX = 80; is a constant that cannot change.
this.name means the name of the object we are inside.

java-four-design-patterns.svg.title: Four friendly design patterns
java-four-design-patterns.svg.caption: Singleton: only one. Factory: a maker. Builder: step-by-step assembly. Observer: a list of listeners that get told. Use them only when they solve a real problem.
steps: Only one object exists, like the school bell. Use rarely.
A method that makes objects: Shape.create("circle").
Make a big object step by step with named settings, then build().
A subject keeps a list of listeners and tells them about changes.
One shared object? Many options? Many listeners? Choose the pattern that fits.
Every pattern adds extra code to read and test.
If a plain constructor is clear, you do not need a pattern.
Names like 'factory' help the team understand quickly.

java-equals-hashcode-and-sorting.svg.title: Same or different? First or last?
java-equals-hashcode-and-sorting.svg.caption: A HashSet uses hashCode to find the right drawer and equals to confirm a match, so the two must agree. A Comparator puts items in the order you choose.
steps: Both say id 1 and title Math.
Objects.hash(id, title) gives the same number for both.
The set jumps to the drawer for that number.
Are they the same? Yes, so the set keeps only one.
Java thinks they are two objects and keeps both.
list.sort(...) needs a rule for which comes first.
A record has correct equals and hashCode for free.
